q: Why must visible organic matter be removed before any soap or disinfectant is applied?
o: It preserves the stainless appearance for public viewing
Most detergents and disinfectants are completely or partly inactivated by organic material such as feces, urine, food and soil
Mechanical removal forces bacteria into resistant spores
Organic debris changes ward humidity and accelerates viral mutation
e: Organic matter physically shields microbes and chemically neutralizes many products, so gross removal must come first.

q: Sanitation is best defined as:
o: Destruction of all pathogens including spores
The manual removal of debris only
The combination of cleaning and disinfection
Application of ultraviolet light to surfaces
e: ASV defines sanitation as cleaning plus disinfection, two separate steps even with a combination product.

q: According to the ASV, true sterilization of cage and kennel surfaces:
o: Is the goal of routine daily cleaning
e: The ASV states plainly that true sterilization of cage and kennel surfaces does not occur; that language belongs to autoclaved instruments.

q: Detergents and degreasers can remove up to what proportion of environmental pathogens before any disinfectant is applied?
e: Detergents break down oil and grime so debris can be rinsed away, removing up to 90% of environmental pathogens.

q: The recommended ASV order of cleaning, from first to last, is:
o: Unhealthy animals, then healthy adults, then puppies and kittens
Healthy puppies and kittens, then healthy adults, then unhealthy animals
By proximity to the front intake office
e: Move from least likely to shed toward most likely, protecting the most susceptible animals.

q: Adequate sanitation CANNOT be accomplished by:
o: Cleaning then disinfecting for the full contact time
Using water alone, or spraying and quickly wiping off a disinfectant
e: Water alone, spray-and-wipe, or a no-detergent disinfectant used without cleaning first all fail to sanitize.

q: Industry guidelines recommend a minimum of how much time per animal per day for routine enclosure cleaning?
e: NACA guidelines cite a minimum of about 9 minutes per animal per day, useful for staffing calculations.

q: Even with a labeled detergent-disinfectant combination product, cleaning and disinfection:
e: Cleaning and disinfection are conceptually and practically separate steps regardless of the product used.

q: The key shelter limitation of quaternary ammonium compounds is that they:
o: Do not reliably eliminate non-enveloped viruses (parvo, panleukopenia, calici) despite label claims
e: Multiple independent studies show quats fail against non-enveloped viruses even when the label claims otherwise.

q: Which statement about sodium hypochlorite (bleach) is accurate?
o: It is effective against FPV, CPV, FCV and ringworm but is inactivated by organic matter and has no detergent action
It stays stable for about 90 days once diluted
e: Bleach is broadly virucidal and fungicidal but has no detergent action and is readily inactivated by organic matter, so cleaning must come first.

q: Once diluted, bleach and calcium hypochlorite remain stable for about:
e: Chlorine dilutions are short-lived (about 24 hours) versus 7 days for potassium peroxymonosulfate and about 90 days for accelerated hydrogen peroxide.

q: Regarding ringworm, potassium peroxymonosulfate (Virkon, Trifectant) is best described as:
o: Effective at about 2% concentration with appropriate contact time
Effective only when used as a footbath
e: The ASPCA Pro reference and ASV list it as effective against dermatophytes at about 2%, correcting the common note that it is ringworm-negative.

q: Which group of products is EFFECTIVE against non-enveloped viruses per the ASPCA Pro reference?
o: Accelerated hydrogen peroxide, potassium peroxymonosulfate, calcium hypochlorite and bleach
e: The oxidizers and chlorine-releasing products clear non-enveloped viruses; quats, biguanides, phenols and alcohols do not reliably do so.

q: Cats are particularly sensitive to which class, which must not be used where cats are housed?
o: Phenols such as Lysol and Pine-Sol
e: Phenolic disinfectants are toxic to cats (feline glucuronyl transferase deficiency slows clearance) and are excluded from cat-housing areas.

q: Which products require NO rinse after the contact time per the ASPCA Pro reference?
o: Accelerated hydrogen peroxide and potassium peroxymonosulfate
e: AHP and potassium peroxymonosulfate are listed as no-rinse, whereas quats, calcium hypochlorite and bleach require rinsing.

q: Several cats develop fever, oral and skin ulceration, ocular lesions and respiratory signs after cage disinfection. The first operational cause to rule out is:
o: Quaternary ammonium compound toxicity from improper dilution or inadequate rinsing
e: Quat toxicity mimics virulent calicivirus; the clue is the cleaning process, and revising it resolves new cases quickly.

q: An enclosure must be completely sanitized (deep cleaned) between different occupants:
o: Even after brief use, even if not visibly soiled, and even if the animal seemed healthy
e: Animals shed pathogens without signs, so a full deep clean is required between occupants regardless of appearance.

q: A documented advantage of spot cleaning for cats is that it:
o: Reduces handling and stress, saves time and chemical, lowers fomite transmission and preserves familiar scent
Eliminates the need for clean bowls
Forces the cat to live in a carrier
e: Spot cleaning is less stressful and lower-risk, and is especially valuable for shy cats and stress-worsened disease such as feline respiratory infection.

q: It is unacceptable to:
o: Spray or hose a primary enclosure while the animal is inside it
Dry the cage before returning the animal
Place a cat in a carrier during deep cleaning
e: Spraying enclosures with animals inside causes distress and contamination; remove animals from nearby compartments when overspray is likely.

q: Mop heads must be:
o: Reused across rooms as long as they stay wet
Disposed of, or sanitized and dried, between uses, including between products and housing areas
Used as the main tool inside cat cages
e: Mops harbor pathogens; ideally mopping is avoided, and mop heads are decontaminated between products and areas.

q: A biological limitation of dishwashers for bowls is that they:
o: Reach high temperatures that destroy most pathogens but may not destroy non-enveloped viruses, so apply a disinfectant after the cycle
e: Heat destroys most pathogens but parvovirus may survive, so a disinfectant step after the cycle is recommended.

q: Recent dermatophyte laundering evidence (Moriello) indicates the most decisive factor for removing Microsporum canis spores from fabric is:
o: Washing twice (mechanical washing and rinsing) without overloading the machine
e: The mechanical double wash is decisive; water temperature and bleach were not the critical variables when items were washed twice.

q: Recommended flooring for the interior of dog kennels is:
o: Resinous epoxy or urethane coatings over concrete (polished sealed concrete suits corridors but not kennels)
e: Epoxy or urethane coatings give a durable, non-porous, disinfectable kennel surface; polished sealed concrete is for high-traffic corridors.

q: Food and water bowls should be sanitized:
o: In the same basin as litter pans to save time
At a different location or time than litter pans to prevent cross-contamination
e: Separating bowl and litter-pan sanitation prevents fecal cross-contamination of feeding items.

q: A fomite is:
o: An inanimate object (hands, clothing, bowls, equipment) that can carry pathogens and transmit disease
e: Fomites are contaminated objects; hands, clothing, bowls, litter boxes, toys and equipment are the everyday shelter examples.

q: The current ASV position on footbaths is that they:
o: Are a reliable primary biosecurity control
Must not be relied on for infectious disease control, because adequate contact time is impractical and organic debris inactivates the disinfectant
Should replace boot changes in isolation
e: The 2022 ASV standard is that footbaths are unreliable and should not be depended on; dedicated boots or disposable covers are preferred.

q: The minimum acceptable hand hygiene station provides:
o: Hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol (a sink with soap, water and single-use towels is ideal)
e: At minimum, at least 60% alcohol sanitizer; ideally a sink with soap, running water and single-use towels.

q: Hand sanitizer (more than 60% alcohol) should be used:
o: On heavily soiled hands during cleaning
Only on hands that are visibly clean, and never as the sole means of hand hygiene
As a substitute for handwashing in all cases
e: Alcohol gels fail on soiled hands and against parvovirus, calicivirus and ringworm, so they are for visibly clean hands and not the sole method.

q: Within the shelter, who is most likely to move pathogens around during daily tasks?
e: Staff handle many animals during care, so their protocols (PPE, hand hygiene) matter most for transmission.

q: Outdoor surfaces such as gravel, dirt and grass:
o: Cannot be disinfected, so covers are rotated or replaced and access is managed
e: These surfaces cannot be disinfected; manage them by rotating covers and restricting access to vaccinated, dewormed, healthy adults.

q: The recommended approach to rodents and insects in the shelter is:
o: An integrated pest management plan, with all food protected in sealed bins and spills cleaned promptly
Ignoring them unless animals get sick
e: Pests harbor pathogens; IPM plus protected food storage reduces both infestation and chemical use.

q: Even with excellent sanitation and facility design, disease control still fails if:
o: The population is not well managed (capacity and flow)
e: Population management underpins biosecurity; no amount of cleaning compensates for crowding and poor flow.

q: The routine contact time for accelerated hydrogen peroxide (AHP, e.g. Rescue) against most shelter pathogens is:
e: AHP's key advantage is a 1-minute contact time for most pathogens (extend to 5 minutes for ringworm). This makes it practical for high-turnover shelter environments where long contact times are not feasible.

q: The correct bleach dilution and contact time for a confirmed CPV (parvovirus) outbreak in a shelter enclosure is:
e: For CPV/FPV outbreaks, bleach should be used at 1:10 (rather than the routine 1:32) with a 10-minute contact time on a pre-cleaned, organic-matter-free surface.

q: A shelter uses bleach at the correct 1:32 dilution but the water temperature in the ward is 5 °C (41°F) in winter. Why might disinfection still fail?
o: Low temperatures can approximately double the contact time needed for disinfectants to achieve their claimed kill, so the standard 10-minute contact becomes inadequate
Cold water prevents bleach from diluting correctly
Bleach must be stored at room temperature or it crystallizes
e: Disinfectant contact times on labels are tested at approximately 20 °C (68°F). In cold environments (< 10 °C (50°F)), effective kill may require approximately double the stated contact time.

q: Which single step in the terminal disinfection sequence is most commonly skipped but cannot be omitted?
o: Relocating animals from the area before starting
Applying the disinfectant at the correct dilution
Completing the detergent wash and thorough rinse before applying disinfectant
e: Organic debris on surfaces will neutralize disinfectants regardless of concentration or contact time. The detergent wash and rinse step must precede disinfectant application — skipping it is the most common reason terminal disinfection fails.

q: What is the required contact time for potassium peroxymonosulfate (Trifectant/Virkon-S) to be effective against Microsporum canis (ringworm)?
e: Potassium peroxymonosulfate requires 10 minutes at 1% concentration for ringworm efficacy. The 5-minute contact time covers general pathogens but is insufficient for dermatophytes.

q: After confirmed CPV in a dog ward, how long must the cleaned, terminally-disinfected cage be held empty before animals can be reintroduced?
o: At least 2 full incubation periods (~14 days)
No empty hold is required — a correctly cleaned and disinfected enclosure can be reused the same day
e: Per the textbook (Karsten, Ch 8), waiting does not add safety: 'the disinfection protocol either was effective or it was not.' A cage correctly cleaned and disinfected with a product effective against parvovirus can be reused immediately; for tough non-enveloped viruses the recommended insurance is to clean and disinfect three times in one day, not to leave the cage empty. The '2 incubation periods' rule is a population-surveillance benchmark for declaring the outbreak resolved, not a cage-holding requirement.
